nodes.text: LangGraph PostgresSaver users report the checkpoint_blobs table growing much faster than the checkpoints table, because the whole messages channel is rewritten each step. Retention needs explicit prune/TTL work. A library that persists full state per step needs a retention and compaction story from day one.
nodes.applicability: LangGraph per-step checkpointing; one user report plus peer replies, no maintainer statement. Does not apply to a store that saves one record per completed turn.
nodes.limitations: Replies came from community members, not LangGraph maintainers. Web-search snippets also mention a 40GB-in-six-weeks postmortem on Towards AI, which could not be fetched (403) and is not cited.

nodes.text: A library upgrade that hardens the checkpoint serializer can make previously storable objects (exceptions, non-Serializable custom objects) fail to serialize. The LangGraph langgraph-checkpoint 3.0.0 change was a deliberate security fix, so custom objects in stored state are a compatibility liability.
nodes.applicability: LangGraph JsonPlusSerializer; single user report with a contributor's explanation, not a maintainer statement.

nodes.text: Pydantic AI guarantees only that V1-serialized message history deserializes in V2. It still changes stored-part semantics between releases: RetryPromptPart is no longer written, old retry parts are reinterpreted on load, and the first request after an upgrade misses the provider prompt cache. A library-owned message format changes over time, and the maintainers need an explicit load-compat layer.
nodes.applicability: Pydantic AI; the changelog shows compat is maintained, not that it breaks. Partly supports the hypothesis that stored histories need versioning or tolerant loading, but no broken-upgrade bug report was found.

nodes.text: Pydantic AI token limits are checked after each model response. The request that crosses the line still completes and is billed, unless count_tokens_before_request=True is set for the per-request input limit. Concurrent runs can each pass the check before any records usage. A cap is therefore a soft bound, not a hard ceiling.
nodes.applicability: Pydantic AI UsageLimits and SpendLimits; two pages from one vendor's docs, so not independent. This is what the documentation states, not a user-reported failure.
nodes.limitations: Same-vendor sources. The count_tokens_before_request detail comes from a summary of the page; the quoted sentence is the verbatim part.

nodes.text: A stream stopped part-way is charged only for the usage the provider had reported by then, which can fall short of the provider's bill. Known token totals for incomplete usage are lower bounds. Reconcile against the provider for exact totals.
nodes.applicability: Pydantic AI SpendLimits (harness); vendor documentation of its own limitation.

nodes.text: In Pydantic AI, request_limit bounds agent-loop turns, not provider requests. Fallback attempts and provider retries do not count toward it, but their tokens and cost still count toward token and cost limits. A fallback chain therefore multiplies spend inside token caps, and a request-count cap does not bound it.

FallbackModel cannot recover from failures above it, such as output parsing or validation failures. A maintainer said it 'cannot automatically retry things that happen upstream from it'. A model-level fallback chain does not cover real-world failure modes that occur after the response is received.
nodes.applicability: Pydantic AI FallbackModel; maintainer replies in a GitHub issue. Does not show fallback masking real bugs.

nodes.text: OpenAI Agents SDK streamed runs had a bug where a tripped output guardrail dropped the function_call/function_call_output pair from the saved session. The next run re-issued the call and the tool ran twice. This is a duplicated side effect caused by session persistence at turn level, fixed in PR 4148.
nodes.applicability: OpenAI Agents SDK sessions with streaming, stop_on_first_tool and output guardrails; a narrow path, fixed upstream.

nodes.text: A crash between a committed external effect and the checkpoint write makes resume repeat the effect, for example a duplicate refund. Checkpoints alone do not make tools safe; the idempotency key must come from durable run state, not the model.
nodes.applicability: General durable-execution argument from a practitioner blog; no measurement or incident data.
nodes.limitations: A single industry source and an illustrative scenario. The LangGraph durable-execution docs page that would give vendor guidance returned 404 and was not read.

nodes.text: OpenAI Agents SDK SQLiteSession created a new lock on every call for file-based databases, so it had no thread safety for file DBs. Only in-memory DBs used the shared lock. A shipped session store therefore lacked concurrency protection until a later fix.
nodes.applicability: SQLiteSession, thread-level safety; does not show two async turns on one session_id being serialized.
nodes.limitations: Content from a PR description summary, not the diff.

nodes.text: LangChain agents' built-in limiters cap call count, not tokens, so a few large calls can consume a very large token volume. Users asked for a token budget. A call-count cap is not a spend cap.
nodes.applicability: LangChain agents, a forum post; the reply was not from a maintainer.

nodes.text: Hypothesis 2 holds: post-response token checks let a single call exceed the cap, so opt-in caps need a pre-request estimate (or a hard per-request max_tokens) if they must be hard, and the typed error must say the cap was crossed by the last call. Docs should say the cap is soft.

Hypothesis 3 is supported but needs refinement. Save-after-completed-turn loses effects of an interrupted turn, and tool side effects can be duplicated on replay (crash window; PR 4148 guardrail path). The design should require idempotency keys for effectful tools, persist tool call and result pairs atomically, and document that a failed turn is replayed from the last saved turn.

Hypothesis 1 is only partly supported. Evidence shows format changes (Pydantic AI retry parts, LangGraph serializer hardening) handled through load-time compat or breaking releases, not user-reported corruption. A versioned envelope with a tolerant reader is a cheap safeguard, but no upgrade-corruption bug report was found.

Is there a reproducible report of two concurrent turns on one session_id corrupting or losing history in Pydantic AI, OpenAI Agents SDK or LangGraph? Searches found only thread-safety and partial-failure bugs.

Is there a concrete bug report that a token limit is bypassed by streaming, or not covered by handoffs or sub-agents in OpenAI Agents SDK? Not found; only Pydantic AI docs on post-response checks and shared usage.
Does a fallback chain mask real bugs or cause cost spikes in practice? Only the docs-level cost accounting (c6) was found, no post-mortem.
